items: Contrast Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and Microservices and explain how the latter evolved from the former.
Apply Domain-Driven Design to discover bounded contexts and define service boundaries.
Distinguish aggregates, entities, and value objects and their role in service design.
Recognize the organizational and operational prerequisites for microservices to succeed.
SOA (Service-Oriented Architecture) — an integration style emphasizing reusable services, often coordinated via an Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) and formal contracts (SOAP/WSDL).
Microservices — small, independently deployable services owning their data, organized around business capabilities, communicating over lightweight protocols.
Bounded Context — a linguistic and semantic boundary within which a particular domain model is valid and consistent.
Ubiquitous Language — a shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts, scoped to a bounded context.
Aggregate — a cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency unit, with one aggregate root.
Context Map — a DDD tool showing relationships (partnership, shared kernel, anti-corruption layer) between bounded contexts.

blocks.text: SOA emerged to break silos by exposing reusable services behind an ESB that handled routing, transformation, and orchestration. In practice, ESBs became heavyweight central bottlenecks, and "services" were often coarse-grained and shared databases. Microservices are a reaction: they keep SOA's service orientation but drop the central bus, favor lightweight protocols (REST, gRPC, messaging), and insist that each service is independently deployable and owns its data. Where SOA optimized for reuse, microservices optimize for replaceability and team autonomy.

The hardest part of microservices is not the technology — it is drawing the boundaries. Domain-Driven Design gives us the key tool: the bounded context. A bounded context is where a specific model and vocabulary hold true. "Customer" means something different in the Sales context (credit limit, orders) than in the Support context (tickets, satisfaction). Trying to force one global "Customer" object across both leads to a distributed monolith. Instead, model two bounded contexts, each with its own model, and connect them explicitly via a context map (e.g., an anti-corruption layer translating between them).

Inside a bounded context, define aggregates: groups of objects that must be consistent together. The aggregate root is the only entry point; invariants are enforced within the aggregate, never across aggregates via distributed transactions. This rule is what makes services independently deployable — a service can guarantee consistency within its aggregate, and accept eventual consistency across aggregates/services. Oversized aggregates cause contention; undersized ones cause consistency bugs. Sizing aggregates is a core architectural skill.

Microservices are an organizational pattern as much as a technical one (Conway's Law). They require mature CI/CD, observability, and teams that can own a service end-to-end. Without these, you inherit distributed-system complexity (network failures, partial outages, data reconciliation) while gaining few of the benefits. Start with a modular monolith and extract services along bounded-context seams only when a real driver appears.
